ann_35.text: This part acts on 107 of 242 training patients (44%); 70 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 57-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, a maximum heart rate of 143 beats per minute, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 85% to about 90% (on the training data only).

Through it, a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 68% to about 48%, and only while the heart rate stays below about 167 beats per minute (on the training data only).

ann_36.text: This part acts only on the 2 of 242 training patients whose thallium result is coded 4; 1 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 52-year-old woman with non-anginal chest pain, an upsloping ST segment and a thallium result coded 4), it raises the predicted risk from below 1% to about 9% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).
Through it, a thallium result coded 4 raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 54% to about 99% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).

ann_37.text: Through this part, atypical angina (about 6%), typical angina (about 9%) and non-anginal chest pain (about 17%) clearly lower a typical patient's predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms (about 54%).
A reversible defect on the thallium scan clearly raises it here, from about 54% to about 88%.

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises it to about 97%, a flat ST segment to about 88%, more ST depression (0 to 2.8 mm) from about 42% to about 82%, higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 37% to about 76%, and older age (42 to 66 years) from about 34% to about 68% (on the training data only).

Fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL raises it to about 65%, and a downsloping ST segment to about 76% (on the training data only; the model has little data on the downsloping ST segment, 17 patients).
Chest pain brought on by exercise raises it only slightly here, from about 54% to about 59% (on the training data only).

ann_38.text: This part acts on 141 of 242 training patients (58%), patients without chest pain on exercise; 47 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 56-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain, no chest pain on exercise, an upsloping ST segment and a normal thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 19% to about 14% (on the training data only).
Through it, being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 54% to about 1%, and a reversible thallium defect lowers it to about 13% (on the training data only).
Atypical angina and chest pain brought on by exercise each raise it here from about 54% to about 64% (on the training data only).
Being a woman clearly lowers the predicted risk, and even more so without chest pain on exercise (from about 54% to about 1%, against no change at about 16% with it).

With chest pain on exercise, atypical angina lowers the predicted risk more (from about 16% to about 1%, against about 54% to about 8% without it), and a downsloping ST segment raises it (from about 16% to about 51%, against about 54% to about 11% without it). The model has little data on this: only 17 training patients (a downsloping ST segment).
